## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Catubyūhahāravibhaṅga* (Ne 9) is an analytical section of the *Nettippakaraṇa* (*Netti*), a post-canonical exegetical treatise preserved within the Pali Khuddaka Nikāya [SuttaCentral]. It provides a detailed analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of the *catubyūha-hāra*—the interpretive method or "mode of conveying a fourfold array." SuttaCentral records an internal passage-level parallel between this section and Ne 5 (*Vicayahāravibhaṅga*) [SuttaCentral].
Reflecting its hermeneutical method of citing and analyzing canonical formulas, the text shares verses and thematic passages with numerous Buddhist works across traditions [SuttaCentral]. Passages within Ne 9 are attested in or linked to the *Dhammapada* (such as Dhp 21 and Dhp 131), the *Udāna* (Ud 2.3 *Daṇḍa Sutta*), the *Jātaka* (Ja 520), parallel Dharmapada and Udānavarga traditions (G-Dhp, Patna Dharmapada, UV 4, UV 30), corresponding Chinese translations (T 210, T 212, T 213), and even external Indian literature such as the *Mahābhārata* and *Manusmṛti* [SuttaCentral].
Text-reuse calculations by DharmaNexus corroborate this dense web of intertextuality, detecting 870 matching passages shared across 63 Pali texts [DharmaNexus]. The heaviest internal overlap occurs with exegetical literature and sibling treatises, foremost the subcommentary *Nettivibhāvinī*, the *Peṭakopadesa* (especially *Hārasampātabhūmi* and *Sāsanapaṭṭhānadutiyabhūmi*), the *Nettippakaraṇa-aṭṭhakathā*, and another section of the *Netti* itself, Ne 37 (*Sāsanapaṭṭhāna*) [DharmaNexus]. Significant reuse is also found with the canonical Nikāyas, notably the *Ekādasakanipāta* (AN 11), *Dasakanipāta* (AN 10), *Tikanipāta* (AN 3), *Saḷāyatana Saṁyutta* (SN 35), and *Khandha Saṁyutta* (SN 22) [DharmaNexus]. In cross-language matches, DharmaNexus aligns sections of the text with Tibetan translations of the *Udānavargavivaraṇa* (D4100) and *Udānavarga* (D4099), as well as the Chinese *Madhyama Āgama* (T 26) [DharmaNexus].
*No discussion of this text was found in the reference-literature corpus; the overview relies on SuttaCentral and DharmaNexus data.*
